svg.aria-label: How a coverage-guided fuzzer discovers the bug that a static analyzer misses, using the Week 2 harness. The target is a function with four nested checks: if byte zero is F, then byte one is U, then byte two is Z, then byte three is Z, it traps; but the byte-three check has no size-greater-than-three guard, so when the input is exactly the three bytes F U Z, reading byte three runs one byte past the buffer and AddressSanitizer reports a heap buffer overflow. A static analyzer reads the code and does not flag this: the path looks reachable and ordinary, and it cannot know the input will ever be exactly F U Z. A coverage-guided fuzzer finds it by running: it mutates inputs and is rewarded whenever a new branch is reached, so instead of blindly guessing it climbs the nested checks one at a time — random bytes, then something starting with F, then F U, then F U Z — and the moment it reaches F U Z the unguarded byte-three read crashes under AddressSanitizer, which writes a crash reproducer file. Bottom line: static tools read the code and miss input-dependent memory bugs; a coverage-guided fuzzer plus a sanitizer discovers them by executing mutated inputs, which is why the two are complements, not substitutes.
svg.title: Fuzzing finds what SAST misses — coverage-guided mutation reaches an unguarded out-of-bounds read (Week 2)
svg.text: Week 2 · coverage-guided fuzzing · the libFuzzer harness in harness.c
The target — four nested checks, one missing guard
When the input is exactly the 3 bytes "FUZ", reading data[3] runs one byte past the buffer.
A static analyzer reads this and stays silent — the path looks normal; it can't know the input will ever be "FUZ".
How the fuzzer gets there — coverage rewards each new branch (not blind luck)
Each new byte matched = new code reached = the fuzzer keeps that input and mutates from it. It climbs the gates.
The crash — caught by the sanitizer, at runtime
The read is only a bug when executed with the triggering input — exactly what a fuzzer + ASan produce.
Static tools read the code and miss input-dependent memory bugs. A coverage-guided fuzzer runs the code on
mutated inputs and a sanitizer catches the fault — so SAST and fuzzing are complements, not substitutes.
